name: International Monetary Fund

summary.text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is an international financial institution conceived at the July 1944 Bretton Woods conference, with 191 member countries. Each member's quota reflects its size in the world economy and determines its voting power and access to IMF resources. IMF lending is conditional: borrowing governments agree to adjust economic policies, with commitments ranging from fiscal and reserve targets to structural reforms, and funds are typically disbursed in installments tied to those actions.

facts.claim: In the 1980s Latin American debt crisis, which began when Mexico said in August 1982 it could not service its debt, the IMF and other official lenders lent countries enough to pay interest on their bank loans in return for structural reforms and deficit cuts. Many cut infrastructure, health and education spending and froze wages; the decade saw high unemployment and falling per-capita income.

sources.title: Latin American Debt Crisis of the 1980s

facts.claim: In the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis, the IMF-supported programs for Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea called for substantial interest-rate increases to stem currency depreciation, restructuring of financial systems, stronger financial regulation, and opening Asian markets to foreign participants, according to IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer.

sources.title: The Asian Crisis and the Changing Role of the IMF (Stanley Fischer)

facts.claim: A 2016 ESMT Berlin study of Greece's first two bailout programmes (about EUR 216 billion from euro-area lenders and the IMF) found that less than 5% (EUR 9.7 billion) went to the Greek fiscal budget. EUR 86.9 billion went to repaying existing debt (including EUR 9.1 billion to the IMF), EUR 52.3 billion to interest payments, EUR 37.3 billion to recapitalizing Greek banks, and EUR 29.7 billion to incentives for private investors to join the 2012 debt restructuring.

sources.title: Where did the Greek bailout money go? (ESMT White Paper WP-16-02)

facts.claim: Thailand: on August 20, 1997 the IMF Executive Board approved support for Thailand of up to about US$4 billion over 34 months as part of a bilateral and multilateral package totalling US$17.2 billion; Thailand drew US$14.1 billion before saying it would not use the remaining balances.
facts.quote: the Executive Board approved support of up to about US$4 billion on August 20, 1997, over 34 months. The total package of bilateral and multilateral assistance to Thailand came to US$17.2 billion

facts.claim: Indonesia: on November 5, 1997 the IMF approved a three-year stand-by credit for Indonesia of up to SDR 7.338 billion (about US$10.14 billion), 490% of quota, with SDR 2.2 billion available immediately and later drawings tied to quarterly performance targets and reviews. The Congressional Research Service put the overall support package announced that day at about US$40 billion (another CRS report gives US$42.3 billion), including US$4.5 billion from the World Bank and a US$3 billion U.S. secondary line of credit. In August 1998 the undrawn balance was converted into an Extended Arrangement.
facts.quote: The stand-by credit authorized drawings of up to SDR 7.338 billion (about US$10.14 billion) to support Indonesia's macroeconomic stabilization and structural reform program

facts.claim: Korea: on December 4, 1997 the IMF Executive Board approved financing for Korea of up to SDR 15.5 billion (about US$21 billion) over three years. The Congressional Research Service put the total international package at about US$58.2 billion (US$57 billion in another CRS report); the IMF share was therefore roughly a third of the headline figure.

facts.claim: Thailand suspended 58 finance companies on June 27 and August 5, 1997 and required each to submit a rehabilitation plan. The Financial Sector Restructuring Authority (FRA), created under emergency decrees alongside an Asset Management Corporation, reviewed the plans and oversaw closures; in December 1997 the FRA and Ministry of Finance announced the closure of 56 of the 58, which the Washington Post reported on December 8, 1997 as a step mandated by the IMF under the US$17.2 billion bailout. The two survivors reopened; the FRA later auctioned the closed companies' assets, selling core loans with a face value of 584 billion baht for 147 billion baht, about 25 percent.
facts.quote: a step mandated by the International Monetary Fund under terms of a $17.2 billion international bailout ... FRA and MOF announced the closure of 56 of 58 finance companies, giving a clear indication of government resolve

facts.claim: Korea's December 3, 1997 letter of intent described the crisis as stemming from an unprecedented number of highly leveraged conglomerates (chaebols) moving into bankruptcy, with financial institutions having priced risk poorly and financed an excessively large share of corporate investment, resulting in high leverage.
facts.quote: unprecedented number of highly leveraged conglomerates (chaebols) moving into bankruptcy ... financial institutions had priced risks poorly and were willing to finance an excessively large portion of corporate investment plans, resulting in high leveraging

sources.title: Korea Letter of Intent, December 3, 1997

facts.claim: Korea's December 1997 stand-by arrangement committed the government to: placing troubled banks under finance-ministry control with rehabilitation plans due in 30 days and licence revocation if not approved; an exit strategy including closures and mergers and acquisitions by domestic and foreign institutions; approving foreign purchases of domestic bank stakes above the 4% limit where they strengthen the sector, with legislation to align equity-purchase rules with OECD practice; replacing blanket guarantees with limited deposit insurance; and measures to reduce corporations' high debt-to-equity ratios and develop capital markets so that banks finance less of corporate investment.
facts.quote: the supervisory authority would approve foreign purchases of domestic bank stakes above the 4 percent limit where they strengthen the sector, and that legislation would be sent to the National Assembly to align equity-purchase rules with OECD practice

sources.title: Republic of Korea: IMF Stand-By Arrangement, December 5, 1997

facts.claim: An IMF staff working paper on Korea's 1997 crisis records that full foreign ownership of merchant banks was allowed from December 1997, that raising foreign ownership and management of banks was seen as a way to recapitalize them, boost competition and improve management, and that cross-guarantees among chaebol affiliates and growth-over-profit strategies had driven unviable investment; it argues that ending widespread cross-guarantees and wider use of consolidated financial statements would have made lending risk easier to see. The documents retrieved commit Korea to reducing corporate leverage and improving transparency; none retrieved requires that chaebol groups be broken up.
facts.quote: Starting in December 1997, full foreign ownership of merchant banks has been allowed

sources.title: The Korean Financial Crisis of 1997: A Strategy of Financial Sector Reform
Republic of Korea: IMF Stand-By Arrangement, December 5, 1997

openQuestions: Korea's later letters of intent (December 24, 1997; February 7, 1998 and after) carry the corporate-governance commitments (cross-guarantees, consolidated statements, debt-to-equity targets). Their text was not retrieved in this session (search budget ran out); the facts above record the December 3, 1997 letter and the stand-by arrangement only. The 'main bank' and 200% debt-to-equity target details seen only in an encyclopedia summary were left out.

Indonesia package totals differ between CRS reports (US$40 billion vs US$42.3 billion) and other accounts (US$18-23 billion of first-line financing); the IMF's own share (SDR 7.338 billion) is the firm figure.
